articles.full_text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

ChatGPT Sites exposure

Pluto researchers combed web archives, public code repositories, search engines and other sources and found 16,666 sites created with ChatGPT Sites (which builds and hosts web apps for ChatGPT and Codex users), 12,830 of which were accessible to anyone. Manual checks confirmed sensitive data exposure at 27 organizations, including a Fortune 500 company’s sales dashboard, a freight forwarder’s customer quotes, and a vendor’s sales pitch. Sites are visible only to their owners and admins unless shared, but owners can open them to the entire internet.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

RansomwareHelp co-founder accused of profiting from ransom payments

US authorities have charged Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a Colombian national and co-founder of the ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, with three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that instead of using its own decryption technology as advertised, his company purchased decryptors from cybercriminals at prices significantly lower than what it charged customers. In one case involving undercover FBI agents, Palacio allegedly paid a $6,000 ransom and billed the purported victim $13,260 for decrypting their files.

USDA payment systems breach

A system used by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make payments to farmers has been breached, according to NBC News. Two former department officials said the intrusion could let hackers access databases containing sensitive information on food safety and diseases carried by animals.

SolarWinds and Adobe patch vulnerabilities

SolarWinds has patched several critical vulnerabilities in its Serv-U managed file transfer product, including flaws that can lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution. Adobe has addressed critical security holes in Campaign Classic and Experience Manager, including ones that allow arbitrary code execution, and a medium-severity DoS vulnerability in InDesign.

Container Store restores systems after cyberattack

US retailer The Container Store has restored its systems following a cyberattack that prevented customers from placing orders online. There is currently no evidence that customers’ financial information was stolen. The n0n ransomware group listed the company on its leak site earlier this month, but The Container Store has not addressed the claim.

VirusTotal adds new ransomware detection capabilities

VirusTotal has introduced new ransomware detection capabilities that rely on evidence of user files being encrypted during sandbox analysis. The improvements include a new behavior tag and stricter requirements for assigning the MITRE ATT&CK technique associated with data encryption for impact. VirusTotal demonstrated the effectiveness of the changes against ransomware that evaded detection by all 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

$17 billion targeted in US government anti-scam operation

The US Justice Department’s crackdown on fraud has targeted more than 800 defendants across over 400 cases since March. Authorities have also helped disrupt scam centers in more than 10 countries. According to the FBI, its Operation Blackout has led to the seizure or restraint of nearly $17 billion.

McDonald’s Japan hacked

McDonald’s Japan has disclosed a breach involving a database storing information associated with its mobile application. Hackers gained access to customer purchase histories, device location information, internal customer identifiers and IP addresses, but not names, contact details or credit card data. The number of impacted customers has not been disclosed.

Bithumb uncovers wider breach

South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says more individuals and more types of personal information were compromised in an October cyberattack than initially reported. Bithumb also said the hackers had access for more than two weeks, not one hour as initially believed. The hackers stole data from an internal collaboration system, including identity documents, bank account numbers, transaction histories, and crypto wallet addresses. South Korean media reported that the initial victim count exceeded 7,000, including customers and staff.

Artex gains traction among state-sponsored hackers

Microsoft has observed several state-sponsored hacking groups, including China’s Salt Typhoon, as well as cybercriminals using the AI-powered penetration testing framework Artex. Hackers have leveraged the tool to identify exposed secrets in public code repositories, conduct supply chain attacks and find vulnerable systems. Microsoft says the framework can significantly accelerate intrusions, with attackers achieving privileged access and establishing persistence within minutes.

Quantum Act targets Europe’s cryptographic readiness

The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act includes measures to accelerate the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography and prepare the EU for the security risks posed by quantum computers. The legislation is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe’s quantum technology industry, reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and establish global leadership in the field by 2030.

Tanker cyberattacks

Up to 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially dangerous cargo are believed to have been targeted in a wave of cyberattacks, according to The Wall Street Journal. US authorities are investigating whether Iran is responsible for the attacks.

Radware hacked

An internal report obtained by BleepingComputer shows that hackers breached cybersecurity firm Radware through an unprotected Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet. Customer contact information and credentials associated with AWS, Azure and SFTP storage used by some customers may have been compromised. The company has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment.

articles.title: Home Office Reprimanded After GDPR Failure at the Border
articles.context: “Our investigation found the Home Office introduced a new system without ensuring staff had a clear, effective process for reporting and correcting inaccurate personal...
articles.full_text:
A major data integrity failure in a new UK border control system led to people being wrongly detained, the country’s data protection regulator has revealed in a reprimand for the government.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) reprimanded the Home Office after finding infringements of Articles 5(1)(d) and 25(1) of the UK GDPR and sections 38(1) and 56(1) of Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018.

They boil down to a failure to ensure the personal information (PII) it processed remained accurate and up to date.

“Our investigation found the Home Office introduced a new system without ensuring staff had a clear, effective process for reporting and correcting inaccurate personal information,” said ICO investigations manager, Joanne Stones.

“That failure could potentially have resulted in serious consequences, including people being wrongly detained for additional checks or refused entry to the UK.”

Read more on Home Office GDPR failures: UK Home Office Breached Data Protection Law with Migrant Tracking Program, ICO Finds

The issue stemmed from the new Helios border control information platform, introduced on October 2 2024. The Home Office failed to put in place a dedicated mechanism for reporting inaccurate personal information, according to the reprimand.

Under the previous system a dedicated team corrected any issues in real time, but the new regime required inaccuracies to be reported to and corrected by the owner of the source data, the ICO said.

Without a system to do so, many of these inaccuracies were left unchecked. Additionally, staff were told not to include PII when filing reports, which the ICO said made it “virtually impossible” to provide the information needed to correct a record.

Over a year later, on October 25 2025, the Home Office introduced a temporary reporting system for inaccuracies in PII. By March the following year, border force officers had raised 6500 incidents through this system, with around 5000 incorrect records removed, the ICO confirmed.

Psychological Distress for Data Subjects

The ICO claimed that these uncorrected inaccuracies in Home Office records led to individuals being wrongly stopped at the border for additional checks.

It said this was likely to cause the “affected individuals psychological distress and potentially result in them experiencing other adverse impacts.”

None have complained to the Home Office since their ordeal, but this may be because the government department never told them about the real cause of their detention at the border, the ICO said.

“Data protection by design is not just about the technology. It’s about making sure the processes, responsibilities, training and safeguards needed to protect people's information are correct from the start,” continued Stones.

“We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay.”

Article 25(1) of the UK GDPR states that organizations must “implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to effectively implement the data protection principles, specifically the accuracy principle.”

NCSC Shares Guidance to Tackle Agentic Threat From ARTEX-Like Tools
articles.context: However, they’ve been rapidly adopted by threat actors to carry out automated attacks at low cost, often in combination with open models or illegal API resellers
articles.full_text:
The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has shared new guidance to help organizations avoid being overwhelmed by the “volume, intensity and duration” of attacks from agentic frameworks like ARTEX.

So-called autonomous offensive frameworks (AOFs) like ARTEX – and Cairn, PentAGI, RedAmon, Xalgorix and Darkmoon – began life as legitimate pen-testing tools designed to probe for weaknesses using a collection of agents.

However, they’ve been rapidly adopted by threat actors to carry out automated attacks at low cost, often in combination with open models or illegal API resellers.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm Infrawatch has tracked 10,848 services across 8105 hosts running AOFs.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) responded to the surge in malicious use of AOFs with new advice published on November 24.

The agency argued that the frameworks are not exploiting novel or even known vulnerabilities, but instead low-hanging fruit like API weaknesses, default or leaked credentials, or misconfigurations in infrastructure as code (IAC).

Read more: FBI Highlights Growing Abuse of AI-Driven Pen-testing Framework ARTEX

The NCSC shared an eight-point plan to help security teams develop a holistic approach to the challenge:

Perform rigorous asset management, including regular reviews and probing of externally accessible infrastructure, in order to understand what’s exposed

Lock down as many services currently accessible from the perimeter as possible, so they can only be accessed by staff or partners. Then harden those that can’t be

Learn to recognize agentic attacks through comprehensive logging across a wide variety of endpoints and parameters. Ensure error messages shown to external users give nothing away that the AOF could use to plan its next move

Identify, prioritize and fix vulnerabilities and misconfigurations within internet-facing assets, using pen testing where appropriate

Deploy “bot challenges” to prevent automated tools abusing services across high-priority assets

Protect at the API level by applying rate limits to accounts, API tokens and authenticated sessions, and monitoring for unusual behavior as well as preventing large volumes of requests

Throttle account creation and sign-ups that use disposable email services, and protect accounts with strong authentication and appropriate access controls. This will help minimize abuse by agents

Place honeytokens or tripwires somewhere no legitimate user would go in order to provide early warning of agentic attacks, use up an agent's time and attempt budget, and keep it away from real assets

The NCSC said AI and agentic defense will in time be the best way to deal with these threats, but programs will take time to mature.

In the meantime, foundational cybersecurity and hygiene should be the priority.

That means putting in place the controls recommended by Cyber Essentials, and following zero trust principles such as identify verification, least privilege, and an “assume breach" mentality.

Critical infrastructure providers in particular should consult the NCSC’s Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) to improve resilience, it added.

articles.title: “Do Good Security” and Other Lessons from Wiz’s FedRAMP VDR & VER Event
articles.context: Wiz recently hosted an event focused around FedRAMP’s new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) requirements
articles.full_text:
Wiz recently hosted an event focused around FedRAMP’s new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) requirements. This event, entitled “The Final Countdown: Supporting FedRAMP VDR & VER Requirements,” brought together industry leaders responsible for maintaining FedRAMP Cloud Service Offerings. With the initial implementation deadline for VDR & VER approaching on December 7th, the event provided a forum to clarify the government's expectations and help cloud service providers navigate the transition from outdated compliance models to modern, continuous security practices.

The centerpiece of the event was an in-depth policy panel featuring subject matter experts from the U.S. Government and leadership from the Cloud Service Providers Advisory Board (CSPAB) alongside Wiz's Head of Government Affairs.

During the discussion, it was emphasized that the core goal of the new policies—often collectively referred to as "VaDER"—is to empower organizations to proactively secure their systems, rather than checking legacy compliance boxes. The panel addressed industry anxieties surrounding compliance timelines, agency reception, and interpretation of the new rules. Following the panel, the event also featured a brief overview and demonstration of the minimal viable product (MVP) capabilities Wiz has introduced to directly support these new VDR requirements, culminating in a Q&A session with industry experts around their operational experiences and lessons learned.

4 Key Takeaways from the Event

Prioritize Real Security Over Compliance: The core philosophy behind the VDR and VER policies is to simply "do good security". Rather than relying on outdated vulnerability scanning, FedRAMP’s VDR & VER requirements focus effective vulnerability detection and response around true risk to agency and customer data.

Embrace the Flexibility: FedRAMP is intentionally avoiding rigid, opinionated guidance on specific tools or methods. This empowers Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) to implement security measures that best fit their unique technical environments, risks, and modern engineering standards.

Pragmatic Deadline Expectations: Panelists discussed details around the upcoming timelines, and discussed how FedRAMP certifications will not be abruptly pulled immediately following the December 7th deadline, provided companies are making a sincere effort to adapt. CSPs will be asked to submit a progress report in December and can utilize corrective action plans for items that require the extended March grace period.

Lead the Way with Agencies: Agency customers may not fully know what to expect from the new reporting formats. CSPs have a unique opportunity to proactively work with their agencies by providing clean, human-readable monthly activity reports that demonstrate the effectiveness of their modern security programs.

Missed the event? Recordings are available

Interested in seeing recordings from the event? Head over to our event summary page to watch the on-demand recordings, hear from government and industry leaders, and see the new Wiz capabilities designed to help your organization accelerate its VDR & VER readiness.

Disclaimer: This content is provided for informational purposes only, does not constitute legal or regulatory advice or imply endorsement by the U.S. Government, FedRAMP, or any third-party organization, and actual compliance outcomes vary by customer environment under a shared responsibility model. Recordings are available for event registrants and other technical practitioners responsible for FedRAMP CSOs who may have missed the registration deadline.

articles.title: AWS achieves Spain’s national Limited Distribution (Difusión Limitada) and NATO Restricted accreditation in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region
articles.context: With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe...
articles.full_text:
Spanish version »

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce that AWS has achieved Spain’s national Limited Distribution (“Difusión Limitada”) and NATO Restricted accreditation for the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation was granted by the Spanish Delegated Authority for the Security of Classified Information, the Secretary of State Director of Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) and the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) are working bodies of the CNI, which audited AWS against the CCN-STIC-004 policy and the applicable ONS requirements.

With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. In Spain, this was a double achievement: AWS first met the national Difusión Limitada requirements and then, in addition to this national methodology, achieved the NATO Restricted accreditation by incorporating the requirements of NATO Directive 32. This demonstrates our continued commitment to helping the public sector, defense, and NATO-affiliated customers run sensitive workloads in the cloud while meeting the highest applicable national and international security requirements.

What this covers

The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation by the CNI confirms that the AWS system in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region meets the procedural and security requirements for handling classified information up to the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted level.

What is Spain’s classified information framework?

Spain’s framework for protecting national classified information is administered by the ONS and the CCN, under the CNI. In 2026, Spain established the framework that enables handling of Difusión Limitada information in the commercial public cloud, under which this accreditation was granted. The accreditation builds on the AWS ENS High certification and the CCN’s IT Product and Service Catalogue (CPSTIC) qualifications. The scope of the accreditation covers the CPSTIC-qualified services and all AWS services certified under ENS High (see the list of AWS services in scope for ENS High). Only the services within this scope that are qualified or certified under the CCN framework (CPSTIC and ENS High) and run in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region can be used for Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted workloads.

What is NATO Restricted?

NATO Directive 32 establishes the security requirements for handling NATO Restricted information in public cloud, and is the directive referenced by Spain’s CCN-STIC-004 policy.

Why this matters to customers

Public sector and defense organizations in Spain can use the AWS Europe (Spain) Region for national Difusión Limitada classified workloads and for NATO Restricted workloads. Under the shared responsibility model, customers that want to process classified information in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region engage the CCN and ONS to accredit their own systems, building on the AWS accreditation.

How to get started

National security and defense customers may build on the AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) to design a cloud architecture for their sensitive workloads. Accreditation documentation is available to eligible customers through AWS Artifact. Customers can also work with their AWS account teams to understand how the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation, and TSE-SE apply to their use cases.

To learn more about AWS compliance in Spain, see the AWS ENS compliance page and the AWS Compliance Programs page.

For more details see AWS NATO Restricted and Difusión Limitada for AWS Europe (Spain) Region web page

Spanish version

AWS obtiene la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted en la Región AWS Europa (España)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido la acreditación nacional de España “Difusión Limitada” y la acreditación NATO Restricted para la Región AWS Europa (España). La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted ha sido concedida por la Autoridad Delegada para la Seguridad de la Información Clasificada de España, la Secretaria de Estado Directora del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). El Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN), y la Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS), son órganos de trabajo del CNI, que auditaron a AWS conforme a la política CCN-STIC-004 y a los requisitos aplicables de la ONS.

Con este hito, AWS se convierte en el primer proveedor cloud acreditado en el nivel NATO Restricted, y en el primero acreditado para Difusión Limitada en la Región AWS Europa (España). En España ha sido un doble logro: AWS cumplió primero los requisitos nacionales de Difusión Limitada y, sobre esta metodología nacional, obtuvo la acreditación NATO Restricted incorporando los requisitos de la Directiva 32 de la OTAN. Esto demuestra nuestro compromiso continuo de ayudar al sector público, a la defensa y a los clientes vinculados a la OTAN a ejecutar cargas de trabajo sensibles en la nube cumpliendo los requisitos de seguridad nacionales e internacionales más exigentes aplicables.

Qué abarca

La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted del CNI confirma que el sistema de AWS en la Región AWS Europa (España) cumple los requisitos procedimentales y de seguridad para tratar información clasificada hasta el nivel Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted.

¿Cuál es el marco español de información clasificada?

El marco español de protección de la información clasificada nacional lo administran la ONS y el CCN, bajo el CNI. En 2026, España estableció el marco que permite tratar información Difusión Limitada en la nube pública comercial, en virtud del cual se ha concedido esta acreditación. La acreditación se basa en la certificación ENS categoría Alta de AWS y en las cualificaciones del Catálogo de Productos y Servicios de Seguridad TIC (CPSTIC) del CCN. El alcance de la acreditación incluye los servicios cualificados en CPSTIC y todos los servicios de AWS certificados en el ENS categoría Alta (consulte la lista de servicios de AWS en el alcance del ENS categoría Alta). Solo pueden utilizarse para cargas de trabajo Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted los servicios de este alcance cualificados o certificados en el marco del CCN (CPSTIC y ENS categoría Alta) que se ejecuten en la Región AWS Europa (España).

¿Qué es NATO Restricted?

La Directiva 32 de la OTAN establece los requisitos de seguridad para tratar información NATO Restricted en la nube pública, y es la directiva a la que hace referencia la política española CCN-STIC-004.

Por qué es importante para los clientes

Las organizaciones del sector público y de defensa en España pueden utilizar la Región AWS Europa (España) para cargas de trabajo clasificadas nacionales Difusión Limitada, así como para cargas de trabajo NATO Restricted. Conforme al modelo de responsabilidad compartida, los clientes que quieran tratar información clasificada en la Región AWS Europa (España) deben dirigirse al CCN y a la ONS para acreditar sus propios sistemas, apoyándose en la acreditación de AWS.

Cómo empezar

Los clientes de seguridad nacional y defensa pueden apoyarse en AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) para diseñar una arquitectura cloud para sus cargas de trabajo sensibles. La documentación de la acreditación está disponible para los clientes elegibles a través de AWS Artifact. Los clientes también pueden trabajar con sus equipos de cuenta de AWS para entender cómo se aplican a sus casos de uso la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted y TSE-SE.

Para más información sobre el cumplimiento de AWS en España, consulte la página de cumplimiento ENS de AWS y la página de Programas de cumplimiento de AWS.

articles.title: Introducing CORNERSTONE: delivering external services for the NCSC

articles.full_text:
The NCSC's existing services have developed strong standards, trusted market relationships and significant reach. But as demand grows, we need to consider how these services can be delivered in ways that are scalable, sustainable, and responsive to the UK’s changing needs.

As a result, the NCSC is exploring how it can modernise the way its external services are designed, delivered and developed. We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and make better use of the capabilities that exist across the cyber security industry.

CORNERSTONE is a multi-year project to develop a more scalable relationship between the NCSC and industry, with each focusing on where it can add most value. Our ambition for CORNERSTONE is not simply to outsource services currently run by the NCSC; we want to make our services more impactful, accessible and adaptable. This will allow the NCSC to focus on those areas where it brings unique insight as the national technical authority for cyber security.

articles.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
articles.context: " The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22
articles.full_text: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

articles.title: Accenture (ACN) Pushes Deeper Into Regulatory Data With AI And Real Time Risk Monitoring
Huntress EU Data Hosting: What Phase 1 Means
articles.context: A first step: ingesting product data in the EU We've already kicked off our EU data hosting initiative, and we're halfway through Phase 1, which will continue through the end of...
articles.full_text:
For some organizations, EU data hosting is a requirement before they can choose a security partner. For others, it may not be required, but is strongly desired. Huntress has gained a significant number of partners and customers in Europe over the last three years, and we're incredibly grateful for their feedback on data hosting and how we can tailor our platform for their unique needs.

We're now actively working toward EU data hosting. But getting there will take time. It requires significant changes to how our platform is built and operated, so we'll move in phases and share more as the work progresses.

Our official EU Data Hosting statement lays out our official plans and serves as the source of truth as they evolve, but this post will cover the basics.

A first step: ingesting product data in the EU

We've already kicked off our EU data hosting initiative, and we're halfway through Phase 1, which will continue through the end of 2026. Here's what that means practically: for newly created accounts that select EU hosting, raw product data collected by supported Huntress products, along with backups, will be ingested and stored in a data center in Frankfurt, Germany. The products in scope are EDR, ESPM, SIEM, ITDR for Microsoft 365, and ISPM for Microsoft 365.

It's important to understand what this first step does and doesn't mean. Phase 1 brings ingestion and storage of raw product data into the EU, but not all processing. Huntress detection and investigation systems will continue to operate in the United States. Data needed for analysis—personal data such as usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, and hostnames—will be transferred to the US for processing. The results of that analysis—including detections (alerts), incident reports, and forensic evidence—will also remain in the US, along with account and billing data.

Phase 1 plan for Huntress EU data hosting

EU hosting will be selected at the account level, so all organizations within an account will use the same region. Existing customers who want EU hosting will need to create a second account. Data already stored in the US won't be moved to the EU during Phase 1.

The bottom line is that Phase 1 brings raw product data and backups into EU storage, while detection and investigation processing and their results remain in the US. We understand this still isn't ideal, which is why we're not stopping here.

What comes next

In Phase 2, we plan to move more of the work itself into the EU. Telemetry and forensic data, along with analysis results such as detections and investigations, would be processed and stored there. Some information would still remain in the US, including certain identifiers used to track and manage detections, as well as account, billing, and contact information. We're also evaluating options for migrating existing customers' historical data.

Phase 2 plan for Huntress EU data hosting

After Phase 2, we'll assess whether even more customer product and personal data should be brought into the EU. That longer-term work is less certain, and we'll define it as we make progress. We aren't committing to timelines for Phase 2 or beyond yet. We'll share more as plans develop.

It's important to note that Huntress will continue to operate a global Security Operations Center (SOC). Authorized team members outside the EU may access EU-hosted data when needed to support customers, respond to incidents, and help maintain the security and availability of our services.

Interested in testing?

If you're a partner or customer interested in taking part in Phase 1 testing, let your Huntress account manager know. We welcome your feedback as we work through this in stages.

For the complete scope and latest details, please refer to the official EU Data Hosting statement (if anything in this post differs from that statement, the statement takes precedence).

articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) could soon be empowered with new authority to investigate and review major cyber incidents affecting national security.

Representatives Morgan Luttrell (R-TX) and Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced a new bill on November 18 that seeks to establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board (NCAI Board) within CISA.

This new board would examine significant cyber incidents affecting US organizations, identify root causes and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future.

The proposed bill, provisionally called the Reviewing Origins, Outcomes, and Threats from Cyber and Artificial Intelligence to Understand Security Events Act (ROOT CAUSE Act), specifies that the NCAI Board would have no regulatory or enforcement authority, and its reviews would not assign civil or criminal liability.

The legislation would establish governance rules covering board membership, conflicts of interest, access to information and the protection of sensitive material. It would also set out criteria for selecting incidents for review, require a majority vote to launch investigations and provide for regular congressional oversight.

Commenting on the legislation introduced through House Homeland Security Republicans, Rep. Luttrell described cyber as “the next phase in the evolution of warfare.”

“As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in this space, it is more critical than ever that we take action,” he added.

Read more: New UK Cyber Monitoring Centre Introduces 'Richter Scale' for Cyber-Attacks

Republican Congressmen Introduce Three Additional AI and Cybersecurity Bills

The proposed ROOT CAUSE Act was among four new bills proposed by Republican representatives of the US Committee on Homeland Security on November 18.

The Improving Nonhuman-Agent Security, Identification, Governance, Handling and Traceability Act (AI INSIGHT Act) would establish a framework for securing AI agents operating on US federal networks, requiring agencies to identify, monitor and control their access to systems and data.

Meanwhile, the Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act (BRIDGE AI Act) would create a CISA pilot program to recruit AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, academia and research institutions to strengthen the agency's technical capabilities.

Finally, the Sector Engagement for Cybersecurity through Unified Responsibility and Expertise in Information Technology Act (SECURE IT Act) would formally designate the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Information Technology Sector, reinforcing its role in coordinating efforts with industry to protect critical technology infrastructure.

In this article

Hackers reportedly breached the FBI’s national crime database

The database held more than 19.3 million records in 2025. How many, if any, were exposed is unknown

If someone calls demanding payment over a warrant, hang up and call the agency directly

The FBI is investigating a reported breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database police use to check for outstanding warrants, identify stolen vehicles, and look up missing-person records.

CNN first reported the breach on November 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation. It is unclear when it happened or how the attackers got in. A law enforcement source confirmed the hack to ABC News. The FBI hasn’t publicly confirmed the incident.

NCIC is a computerized database that local, state, and federal agencies can all use. It holds records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. Police officers use it during traffic stops, investigations, and background checks.

The system held more than 19.3 million records in fiscal year 2025. It’s still unclear whether anyone stole data. The database includes the following types of records:

Wanted-person and warrant records

Missing-person records

Criminal history data

Protection orders

Records of stolen vehicles, firearms, and other property

NCIC is one of the databases the FBI checks during firearm background checks. The reports do not say that attackers breached the background-check system itself or that gun buyers’ information was exposed.

If someone stole NCIC data, people who could be affected include those with past arrests, people with protection orders, missing people and their families, and victims of crime. Possible risks include the following:

Exposure of sensitive records. Criminals could use criminal history or details from protection orders for harassment, extortion, or doxxing.

Targeted scams. Scammers could pose as police officers and use details from a real warrant to make a demand for payment sound convincing.

Data enrichment. Records from other sources could be linked to the data in this database, providing attackers with more details to make their messaging believable.

This is the second reported intrusion involving FBI systems in about two months. FBI employees whose information was exposed in the September breach face risks including phishing and identity theft. CNN reported that some felt left in the dark about whether they were affected.

How to stay safe

If you feel your data might be involved, here are some steps you can take while we learn more about the breach:

Be wary of unsolicited calls, emails, or messages from police or the FBI. Law enforcement won’t demand gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers.

Be wary of breach notification emails and texts. Don’t click links. Go to official sites directly.

Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication on your accounts. Passkeys are even better where they’re offered as an option.

Check your own online exposure with a tool like Malwarebytes’ Digital Footprint scan, and keep your devices updated.

Once more information or an official confirmation becomes available, we’ll keep you posted.

If your data was involved in a breach, read our guide for more advice: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.context: But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers
articles.full_text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: Europe’s 2027 Cyber Compliance Year: What’s Fixed, What’s Moving, and What One Incident Looks Like Under Four Laws
articles.context: DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review
articles.full_text:
On Dec. 11, 2027, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, and every new connected product placed on the European market will need security built in and a CE mark to prove it. That is the date most 2027 planning decks lead with. It is also the only big date of the year that is truly fixed.

Around it, almost everything else is in motion. NIS2 is being amended while three member states still haven't passed it. DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review. The UK's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is weeks or months from becoming law, with its duties phased in after that.

So the useful question for 2027 isn't "what's due when?" It's "which of these dates can I build on, which might move, and which depend on things that aren't ready yet?" This 2027 cyber compliance guide sorts all four regimes that way. It then follows a single cyber incident through all four laws at once, because that is where the overlap actually hurts.

The four laws in brief

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) regulates products: hardware and software with digital elements sold in the EU. Manufacturers must design them securely, handle vulnerabilities for a set support period and report actively exploited flaws.

NIS2 regulates organizations: "essential" and "important" entities in 18 sectors, from energy and health to managed IT services. It requires risk-management measures, incident reporting and accountability for senior management. As a directive, it works through national laws.

DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, regulates the financial sector's ICT resilience. It has applied since January 2025, and for banks, insurers and other financial entities it takes precedence over NIS2. It also lets EU financial supervisors oversee critical tech providers directly.

The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill updates the UK's 2018 NIS Regulations. It brings managed service providers, data centres and designated critical suppliers into scope for the first time and tightens incident reporting. It doesn't apply in the EU, and the EU laws don't apply in the UK, but a UK company selling products or services into the EU can face all four.

What's fixed: the dates you can build on

These are in force or set in law, and nothing on the legislative calendar is likely to move them.

CRA reporting is already live. Since Sept. 11, 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting their products: an early warning within 24 hours and a fuller notification within 72, submitted through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The European Commission is explicit that this covers products already on the market, not just new ones. If your 2027 plan still lists CRA reporting as a future task, it's a year late.

The CRA applies in full on Dec. 11, 2027. From that date, the essential security requirements, technical documentation, software bill of materials (SBOM) and CE marking apply to products placed on the EU market. Products already on sale before then are caught by these requirements only if they are substantially modified afterwards. Open-source software stewards also pick up reporting duties on the same day.

DORA's first testing cycle closes in January 2028. Financial entities designated as significant must run threat-led penetration testing at least every three years. DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025, so the first cycle runs out in January 2028, and 2027 is when most of those tests will happen. Each one involves live production systems and often the entity's critical tech suppliers.

NIS2 is live in 24 member states. Where a national law is in force, the obligations already apply: registration, risk-management measures, 24-hour early warnings for significant incidents and management accountability. 2027 isn't a NIS2 start date for most of the EU. It's the second year of supervision.

Talk to Cyble about 2027 Cyber Compliance readiness and see how exploitation intelligence fits into your CRA and NIS2 reporting process.

What's moving: rules being rewritten while you comply

NIS2 is being amended before it's finished. France, Ireland and Spain still had no national NIS2 law in force in November 2026, and the Commission referred late countries to the EU Court of Justice in July. France's National Assembly passed its bill at first reading on Nov. 17, 2026; it still needs a joint committee of both chambers.

Meanwhile, the Commission's January 2026 amending proposal would add a small mid-cap category that moves many companies from "essential" to "important," standardize ransomware reporting data and let a cyber posture certificate count as proof of compliance. The Commission is aiming for political agreement in early 2027, and member states would then have a year to transpose the changes. Plan against today's national law; budget for a second update in 2028.

The Cybersecurity Act is being replaced. The same package proposes a new Cybersecurity Act (often called CSA2) that would let the EU name third countries that pose a cyber risk and restrict high-risk suppliers of key ICT assets used by NIS2 entities. If adopted in the form proposed, that becomes a supply-chain question for every NIS2 organization.

Incident reporting may get a single front door. The Digital Omnibus simplification package proposes one entry point for reporting incidents under several EU laws. The Council's Oct. 21, 2026 position favors a national single entry point in each country plus an EU information point run by ENISA. It's still a proposal, so the separate channels remain the ones that count in 2027.

DORA's supervised-provider list is due for review. EU financial supervisors designated 19 critical ICT third-party providers, including AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud, in November 2025, and are expected to reassess the list during 2027 using 2026 data. A provider that lands on it gets direct EU oversight; its financial-sector customers get new contract and exit-planning questions.

The UK Bill is close but not yet law. The House of Lords finished with the Bill on Nov. 2, 2026, and it went back to the Commons over two amendments peers had made. Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties then arrive through secondary legislation, and a House of Lords Library briefing says commencement may run through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the Information Commission (the renamed ICO).

What depends on infrastructure that may be late

The CRA's Dec. 11, 2027 date is fixed. What isn't fixed is whether the machinery for meeting it will be ready.

Harmonised standards. Most manufacturers would prefer to show compliance by applying harmonised European standards, which give a legal presumption of conformity. As of late August 2026, no CRA harmonised standard had been cited in the EU's Official Journal for any product category, and the cross-product standard covering all the essential requirements isn't due until 2027.

Notified bodies. Products in the CRA's "important class II" and "critical" categories need a third-party assessment from a notified body. So do "important class I" products, such as password managers, VPNs, browsers and smart home devices, unless the manufacturer fully applies a harmonised standard or certification scheme. The rules for designating these bodies have applied since June 11, 2026, but none had been designated by late June, and the target of having enough of them by Dec. 11, 2026 is a best-efforts goal.

Put those together and the practical deadline for many manufacturers is earlier than December 2027. If a class I product can't rely on a published standard, it may need a notified body, and assessment slots are likely to fill up well ahead of the deadline. The safe assumption is that standards arrive late and assessors are scarce: start the technical file and risk assessment now, and book an assessor as soon as one is designated for your product category.

One incident, four clocks

Comparison tables make these laws look like separate tracks. They stop being separate the moment something goes wrong. Here is a single, hypothetical incident and every reporting clock it starts.

The setup. A UK-headquartered managed service provider runs IT for European customers, including a bank in the EU. It also sells its own remote-management agent, the software installed on every customer machine it looks after. At hour zero, it discovers that attackers used an unknown flaw in that agent to push ransomware across several client networks, including the bank's.

Clock 1: DORA, for the bank. The bank must decide whether this is a "major" ICT incident. If it is, the initial notification to its financial supervisor is due within four hours of that decision and no later than 24 hours after the bank became aware. An intermediate report follows within 72 hours of the initial one, and a final report within a month after the last intermediate report. The bank can't write any of them without facts from the provider, which is why DORA requires ICT contracts to include help during incidents.

Clock 2: NIS2, for the provider. Managed service providers are in scope of NIS2. A provider based outside the EU that serves EU customers must name a representative in a member state and answers to that country's authority. For a significant incident, NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within a month.

Clock 3: the CRA, for the provider as a manufacturer. The flaw is in a product the provider sells, and it's being actively exploited. Under the CRA, that means an early warning within 24 hours, a vulnerability notification within 72 hours and a final report within 14 days of a fix being available, all through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The provider must also tell affected users.

Clock 4: the UK Bill, once commenced. As a medium or large managed service provider, the company would also owe the UK regulator an initial notification within 24 hours and a full report within 72. If personal data was exposed, GDPR's 72-hour breach notification makes it five clocks.

One hypothetical incident: reporting deadlines under DORA, NIS2, the CRA and the UK Bill

Three lessons fall out of the timeline. First, the earliest deadline belongs to the customer, not the company that was breached: the bank's four-hour clock depends on information from the provider, so provider contracts need a customer notification commitment measured in hours, not days. Second, each law uses a different trigger, whether "major," "significant" or "actively exploited," so the same event can be reportable under one law and not yet under another. Third, the facts are the same in every report. Keep one incident record and map it to each format, rather than writing four reports from scratch at 3 a.m.

Reality check: what enforcement actually looks like

Search for NIS2 or DORA fines and you'll find confident lists of six-figure penalties. Most can't be traced to a regulator. Here is what can, alongside claims that keep circulating.

Claim

Status

What the record shows

Austria's FMA fined Western Union International Bank €42,000 under DORA (July 14, 2026)

Verified

Repeatedly late incident reports under DORA's reporting rules

Romania's DNSC fined a public body 50,000 lei, about €10,000, under NIS2 (Sept. 29, 2026)

Verified

Missing the deadline to notify the authority that it was in scope

Germany's BSI fined a cloud provider €850,000 under NIS2 (February 2026)

Not traceable

Widely repeated; independent trackers found no published NIS2 fine as of July 2026

"Most CRA obligations apply from September 2027"

Wrong

Reporting applied from Sept. 11, 2026; everything else from Dec. 11, 2027

"DORA's compliance deadline is in 2026"

Wrong

DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025

Two lessons. The first verified fines are about process, not breaches: a late report and a late registration. Supervisors are starting with the obligations that are easiest to prove, so registration deadlines and reporting clocks are where 2027 risk is most concrete. And the ceilings, up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover for essential entities under NIS2, are a long way from any penalty actually imposed so far. Use the ceilings to size the risk, not to predict the bill.

A 2027 plan in six moves

Map exposure by entity and by product. NIS2, DORA and the UK Bill attach to what your organization is. The CRA attaches to what it sells. A UK software company with EU banking customers can be inside all four. List every legal entity and every product, then the regimes each one triggers.

Build one reporting matrix and rehearse it. For each regime, record the trigger, the deadline, the recipient and the format. Then run the four-clock scenario above as a tabletop exercise and time how long it takes to decide whether an incident is "major," "significant" or "actively exploited."

Rewrite supplier contracts around hours. Your customers' clocks may start before yours. Agree customer notification times in hours, make sure financial-sector contracts carry DORA's required incident-assistance terms, and require component suppliers to tell you about exploited vulnerabilities fast enough for your own CRA reporting.

Run the CRA as two projects. Reporting is live and operational. Product compliance is a December 2027 engineering project: risk assessments, technical files, SBOMs, support periods and, for some products, a notified body. Don't let the second wait on the first.

Build to today's law and watch the drafts. Comply with the national NIS2 law in force now, and track the amendments, CSA2's supplier restrictions, DORA's provider review and the UK's commencement regulations without engineering to drafts that may change.

Get registrations right. The first verified NIS2 fine was for a missed registration notice. Check NIS2 registration in every country where you operate, and if you're a UK managed service provider, have your registration ready for the three-month window after commencement.

The question that starts the CRA clock

One phrase in the CRA deserves more attention than it gets: "actively exploited." A vulnerability in your product isn't reportable just because it exists. The 24-hour clock starts when you know it's being used in attacks. That knowledge rarely comes from inside your own engineering team. It comes from exploitation seen in the wild, chatter on criminal forums, proof-of-concept code and attacks on other organizations running the same component.

That makes threat intelligence a compliance input, not just a security one. Cyble tracks vulnerability exploitation, dark web activity and attacker infrastructure across the open, deep and dark web, which is the evidence a manufacturer needs to know when its clock has started and to show regulators why it reported when it did.

Frequently asked questions

What cyber compliance deadlines fall in 2027?

The main fixed date is Dec. 11, 2027, when the EU Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, including essential security requirements, SBOMs and CE marking for products placed on the EU market. DORA's first three-year cycle of threat-led penetration testing also runs through 2027 and ends in January 2028. NIS2 amendments and the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's commencement are expected but not yet fixed.

Do UK companies have to comply with the CRA, NIS2 and DORA?

Yes, if they sell into the EU. The CRA applies to any product with digital elements placed on the EU market, wherever the manufacturer is based. NIS2 can apply to UK providers serving EU customers, which must appoint an EU representative. DORA applies to EU financial entities and reaches UK tech providers through contracts and, for critical providers, direct oversight.

When will the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill take effect?

Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties will then be brought in by secondary legislation, possibly in phases through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the regulator.

Does DORA replace NIS2 for banks?

For financial entities, DORA is the sector-specific law and takes precedence over NIS2 on ICT risk management, incident reporting, testing and third-party risk. A bank reports major ICT incidents under DORA's timelines, not NIS2's.

Has anyone been fined under NIS2 or DORA?

Yes, but the verified fines are small. Austria's financial regulator fined a bank €42,000 under DORA in July 2026 for late incident reports, and Romania's cybersecurity directorate fined a public body about €10,000 under NIS2 in September 2026 for a late registration notice.
